title: Signal Detection Theory (d-prime) for Judge Discrimination vs Bias
quick_reasoning: Disentangles judge sensitivity from bias, precise oversight-error characterization.

original_idea.body:
# Signal Detection Theory (d-prime) for Judge Discrimination vs Bias

**Problem:** Judge accuracy conflates two things: ability to discriminate good from bad arguments, and a response bias toward accepting/rejecting. Oversight research rarely separates them.

**Direction:** Apply signal detection theory from psychophysics. From a weak judge's accept/reject decisions on correct vs flawed arguments, compute d-prime (sensitivity) and criterion c (bias). Show how two judges with equal accuracy differ in exploitability, and how prompt changes move sensitivity vs bias. Pure analysis on judge outputs from an open model.

**Why it matters:** Disentangling sensitivity from bias tells us whether an overseer is exploitable via its decision threshold, a precise, training-free characterization of systematic oversight error.

**Relevant context:** Signal detection theory (d', criterion) from cognitive science. Automation/confirmation bias in evaluators (arXiv:2507.19486; arXiv:2010.07938). Open problem: characterize biases overseers consistently exhibit (Anthropic).

title: System-Prompt Hardening Effect Meter
quick_reasoning: Measures safety/utility tradeoff of system-prompt defenses against jailbreaks.

original_idea.body:
# System-Prompt Hardening Effect Meter

**Problem:** Practitioners add safety instructions to system prompts hoping to harden models, but there is no standardized measurement of how much a given system-prompt intervention actually reduces jailbreak ASR vs how much it increases over-refusal.

**Direction:** Build a harness that takes a library of candidate system-prompt safety templates and, for each, plots the (jailbreak-ASR reduction, over-refusal increase) trade-off point using StrongREJECT (harmful) + XSTest (benign) on open models. Output a Pareto frontier of system-prompt interventions.

**Why it matters:** System-prompt hardening is the cheapest, most accessible 'defense' available to anyone deploying open models, but its safety/utility trade-off is unmeasured and easily over-claimed. A Pareto tool gives evidence-based guidance. Pure inference, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** XSTest (arXiv:2308.01263) for over-refusal; StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) for jailbreak scoring. Context open problem: 'adaptive defenses that maintain robustness without catastrophic over-refusal' — the trade-off is the crux.

title: Epidemiological Sensitivity/Specificity Framing for Oversight Screening
quick_reasoning: Base-rate-aware evaluation of oversight as a screening test for rare misbehavior.

original_idea.body:
# Epidemiological Sensitivity/Specificity Framing for Oversight Screening

**Problem:** Oversight protocols are screening tests for 'is this output bad', but we rarely report sensitivity, specificity, PPV/NPV at realistic base rates of misbehavior, so headline accuracy misleads.

**Direction:** Transfer the diagnostic-test evaluation framework from epidemiology. Treat a weak judge as a screening test; on a labeled set of good/bad outputs, compute sensitivity, specificity, and PPV/NPV swept across plausible (low) misbehavior base rates. Visualize how a 'good' judge becomes near-useless when bad outputs are rare. Pure analysis.

**Why it matters:** Realistic base rates of rare strategic misbehavior are exactly the long-horizon regime labs underweight; a base-rate-aware oversight evaluation is high counterfactual value and needs no special resources.

**Relevant context:** Sensitivity/specificity/PPV and base-rate effects from diagnostic epidemiology. LLM-as-judge reliability under class imbalance (arXiv:2412.12509 uses kappa for imbalance). No standardized oversight benchmark exists (context gap).

title: Devil's-Advocate Red Team from Organizational Decision Theory
quick_reasoning: Tests structural intervention against confirmation bias in oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Devil's-Advocate Red Team from Organizational Decision Theory

**Problem:** Single-pass oversight inherits the judge's confirmation bias; the judge tends to seek arguments confirming its initial lean.

**Direction:** Import the institutionalized 'devil's advocate' / dialectical inquiry method from organizational decision science. Implement a two-stage oversight where a second instance of the SAME weak model is forced to construct the strongest case against the first's tentative verdict before final judgment. Measure confirmation-bias reduction on a debate set vs single-pass. Training-free.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether a cheap structural intervention from group decision-making counteracts a documented oversight bias (confirmation bias), directly addressing a named scalable-oversight challenge.

**Relevant context:** Devil's advocacy / dialectical inquiry counter groupthink in decision science. Confirmation bias as scalable-oversight challenge (arXiv:2507.19486). Self-critique listed among oversight protocols (search synthesis).

title: Fault-Tree Analysis to Map Oversight-Protocol Failure Paths
quick_reasoning: Systematic failure-mode map for oversight protocols, well-targeted safety engineering.

original_idea.body:
# Fault-Tree Analysis to Map Oversight-Protocol Failure Paths

**Problem:** We discuss oversight failures anecdotally but lack a systematic enumeration of the conjunctive/disjunctive failure paths by which a protocol lets a bad output through.

**Direction:** Borrow fault-tree analysis from reliability/safety engineering. Construct a fault tree for a concrete debate protocol (top event: bad output approved) decomposing into basic events (judge anchors, debater colludes, decomposition loses info), then estimate basic-event probabilities from small empirical probes on an open model and compute the top-event probability. Deliverable is the empirically-parameterized fault tree.

**Why it matters:** Provides a reusable, quantitative failure-mode map for oversight protocols, the kind of safety-engineering rigor usually absent, buildable with no lab resources and addressing FR68 (systematic failure-mode characterization).

**Relevant context:** Fault-tree analysis from systems-safety engineering; five-recipes-for-formal-verification of autonomous systems (arXiv:2012.00856). Benchmark for scalable oversight protocols (arXiv:2504.03731). FR68 surprising-result follow-up.

title: Test-Retest Reliability for Judge Stability Under Resampling
quick_reasoning: Foundational reliability measurement for oversight verdicts.

original_idea.body:
# Test-Retest Reliability for Judge Stability Under Resampling

**Problem:** LLM judge verdicts vary across seeds, but oversight papers often report a single run; we lack a psychometric reliability estimate for how reproducible a judge's oversight is.

**Direction:** Apply test-retest and intraclass-correlation reliability from psychometrics. Run a weak judge multiple times (varied seed/temperature/order) over the same debate items and compute test-retest reliability and ICC, then relate low reliability items to error-prone categories. Pure inference, cheap to run many times on a small model.

**Why it matters:** Establishes whether oversight verdicts are even reliable enough to trust before asking if they are valid, a foundational measurement contribution any group can produce and labs rarely report.

**Relevant context:** Test-retest reliability/ICC from psychometrics; inter-rater reliability sensitive to seed variation in LLM judges (arXiv:2412.12509). Kenton et al. 2024 judge setup. No standardized oversight benchmark (context gap).

title: Forecasting Calibration Tournaments for Comparing Oversight Protocols
quick_reasoning: Standardized comparison harness filling an oversight-benchmark gap.

original_idea.body:
# Forecasting Calibration Tournaments for Comparing Oversight Protocols

**Problem:** Debate, consultancy, and direct-QA are compared on accuracy, but there is no standardized tournament-style calibration comparison, and no standardized oversight benchmark exists.

**Direction:** Transfer the structure of forecasting tournaments (Good Judgment Project style: many questions, proper-score leaderboard, calibration tracking). Build a small fixed question set and run several oversight protocols on one open model, scoring each by Brier/log score and calibration, producing a reproducible mini-tournament harness and leaderboard.

**Why it matters:** Creates a lightweight, shareable standardized comparison harness for oversight protocols, filling the explicitly-identified benchmark gap with no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Forecasting tournaments and proper-score leaderboards (Tetlock/Good Judgment lineage); proper scoring rules (arXiv:1212.5764). A Benchmark for Scalable Oversight Protocols (arXiv:2504.03731). 'No standardized scalable oversight benchmarks exist' (context).

title: Linguistic Hedging/Deception Cues from Forensic Linguistics as Oversight Features
quick_reasoning: Feature-based aid for detecting persuasive-but-wrong arguments in oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Linguistic Hedging/Deception Cues from Forensic Linguistics as Oversight Features

**Problem:** Weak judges weigh surface fluency; they ignore linguistic markers (hedging, evasion, distancing language) that forensic linguistics associates with low-confidence or deceptive statements.

**Direction:** Import statement-analysis cue catalogues from forensic/deception linguistics. Extract simple lexical features (hedges, qualifiers, pronoun distancing, vagueness) from debater turns and test whether they predict which side is actually wrong on a labeled debate set, then test if surfacing these cues to a weak judge improves verdicts. Feature extraction + small logistic model.

**Why it matters:** A cheap, interpretable feature-based aid for overseers that needs no model internals, helping detect persuasive-but-wrong arguments, a counterfactually valuable, infrastructure-light contribution.

**Relevant context:** Forensic linguistics deception/hedging cues (statement analysis literature). Persuasion-over-truth risk in consultancy (Kenton et al. 2024). Bias in how humans evaluate AI suggestions (arXiv:2509.08514).

title: Ensemble Diversity Metrics (Ecology) to Predict Panel-Oversight Gains
quick_reasoning: Predictor for when panel oversight beats single judge, relevant to recursive oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Ensemble Diversity Metrics (Ecology) to Predict Panel-Oversight Gains

**Problem:** Stacking multiple weak judges only helps if their errors are diverse; we lack a principled, pre-deployment measure of judge-error diversity to predict whether a panel will beat a single judge.

**Direction:** Borrow diversity indices from ecology/ensemble theory (e.g., disagreement measure, Q-statistic, error-correlation). Compute error-diversity among several prompt/temperature variants of one open judge, then test whether higher measured diversity predicts larger accuracy gains from majority-vote panels on a debate set. Pure analysis.

**Why it matters:** Tells oversight designers when panel/recursive aggregation is worthwhile vs wasted, with a measurable predictor, useful and resource-light, relevant to recursive oversight feasibility.

**Relevant context:** Ensemble diversity measures (Q-statistic, disagreement) from ML/ecology; ensembles beat majority vote only with decorrelated errors (Machine Truth Serum arXiv:1909.13004 background). Recursive oversight open problem (Anthropic).

title: Contract-Based Design: Pre/Post-Conditions for Sub-Delegated Oversight
quick_reasoning: Localizes failures in recursive oversight via interface contracts, well-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Contract-Based Design: Pre/Post-Conditions for Sub-Delegated Oversight

**Problem:** In recursive/amplified oversight, a top judge delegates sub-questions but cannot verify the sub-answers; errors propagate silently through delegation.

**Direction:** Transfer design-by-contract (preconditions/postconditions/assertions) from formal software engineering. Require each delegated sub-task to ship explicit machine-checkable postconditions (e.g., 'answer must be one of {A,B}', 'must cite a provided source'); a lightweight contract checker validates sub-answers before they feed the parent judge. Prototype a 2-level decomposition on QA with an open model and measure caught violations.

**Why it matters:** Brings interface-contract discipline to recursive oversight so failures are localized rather than propagated, a concrete safe-harness prototype with no lab dependency.

**Relevant context:** Design-by-contract (Meyer; pre/post-conditions) from software engineering; VeriGuard verifies actions against policies (arXiv:2510.05156); AGENT-C constraint enforcement (arXiv:2512.23738). Iterated amplification / recursive oversight (OpenAI, Anthropic).

title: Item Difficulty Curves to Find Where Weak-to-Strong Oversight Breaks
quick_reasoning: Maps the difficulty frontier where weak-to-strong oversight breaks.

original_idea.body:
# Item Difficulty Curves to Find Where Weak-to-Strong Oversight Breaks

**Problem:** Weak-to-strong generalization breaks down as capability gaps grow, but we lack a fine-grained, item-level map of the difficulty frontier where weak judges stop tracking truth.

**Direction:** Borrow dose-response/difficulty-curve modeling from pharmacology/psychometrics (without re-using already-covered IRT framings). Treat per-item difficulty (estimated cheaply from strong-model confidence or human-rated complexity) as the 'dose' and judge accuracy as 'response'; fit a curve and locate the breakdown threshold for several open judge sizes. Pure analysis on existing labeled items.

**Why it matters:** Gives a quantitative breakdown-threshold characterization of weak-to-strong oversight, directly answering 'when can weaker models reliably supervise stronger ones', achievable on a consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Dose-response curve fitting from pharmacology. Weak-to-strong breakdown at large gaps (Kenton et al. 2024; OpenAI weak-to-strong, open code per context). Distinct from already-covered IRT person-fit / dose-response capability-elicitation ideas.

title: Audit Sampling (Accounting) for Cost-Efficient Oversight Coverage
quick_reasoning: Budget-aware sampling policy for catching rare misbehavior in oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Audit Sampling (Accounting) for Cost-Efficient Oversight Coverage

**Problem:** Reviewing every agent output with a careful overseer is too expensive at scale, but naive random spot-checks miss concentrated misbehavior; oversight lacks a principled sampling policy.

**Direction:** Import statistical audit sampling from accounting/auditing (e.g., monetary-unit / risk-weighted sampling). Define a risk score per agent output (cheap heuristic), then compare random vs risk-weighted vs stratified audit sampling for catching planted bad outputs at a fixed review budget. Simulation + small empirical study on an open model.

**Why it matters:** Audit-sampling theory gives oversight a budget-aware coverage policy for rare misbehavior, a practical scaling tool with strong counterfactual value (no lab infra needed).

**Relevant context:** Statistical/monetary-unit audit sampling from accounting & auditing standards. Rare-misbehavior base-rate problem (diagnostic-test framing). Reward-hacking-of-overseer priority (Open Phil RFP); market-making oversight (arXiv:2511.17621).

title: Contrastive Over-/Under-Refusal Joint Scorecard
quick_reasoning: Unified safety/helpfulness frontier metric, directly safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Contrastive Over-/Under-Refusal Joint Scorecard

**Problem:** Safety benchmarks (StrongREJECT) and over-refusal benchmarks (XSTest, OR-Bench) are run separately, so no single artifact reports a model's joint position on the safety/helpfulness frontier with one comparable metric.

**Direction:** Define a single 'refusal calibration' scorecard combining harmful-refusal-rate (from StrongREJECT/AILuminate) and benign-refusal-rate (from XSTest/OR-Bench) into one F-style discrimination metric, then compute it for several open models and rank them. Ship the unified harness so any model can be plotted on the same axes.

**Why it matters:** The field treats over-refusal and under-refusal as separate problems; a unified scorecard makes the inherent trade-off explicit and comparable, directly serving the 'no catastrophic over-refusal' open problem. Combines existing public datasets; no training.

**Relevant context:** OR-Bench (2025, 80K over-refusal prompts), XSTest (arXiv:2308.01263), StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260), AILuminate (arXiv:2503.05731). Context open problem on avoiding catastrophic over-refusal.

title: Triangulation from Mixed-Methods Research to Combine Heterogeneous Oversight Signals
quick_reasoning: Recipe for fusing fallible oversight signals into a more robust verdict.

original_idea.body:
# Triangulation from Mixed-Methods Research to Combine Heterogeneous Oversight Signals

**Problem:** Oversight signals come in different forms (judge verdict, consistency check, calibration, linguistic cue) but are usually used in isolation; we lack a principled way to combine heterogeneous, partially-valid signals.

**Direction:** Transfer the 'triangulation' principle from mixed-methods social science: convergent validity across methodologically independent measures raises confidence. Combine 3-4 cheap, independent oversight signals on each output and test whether agreement-based triangulation improves detection of bad outputs over any single signal and over naive averaging, on an open-model debate/QA set.

**Why it matters:** A simple, theory-grounded recipe for fusing fallible oversight signals into a more robust verdict, lab-independent and directly relevant to building robust recursive oversight.

**Relevant context:** Triangulation / convergent validity from mixed-methods research methodology. Combining oversight protocols (market-making vs debate, arXiv:2511.17621; multi-agent debate for error detection, arXiv:2510.20963). Recursive-oversight-with-systematic-errors open problem (Anthropic).

title: Behavioral Game-Theory Schelling Probes for Implicit Judge-Debater Coordination
quick_reasoning: Probes implicit coordination/collusion undermining oversight, medium-horizon threat.

original_idea.body:
# Behavioral Game-Theory Schelling Probes for Implicit Judge-Debater Coordination

**Problem:** Strategic models could coordinate on a focal wrong answer without explicit communication; we have no cheap probe for such Schelling-point coordination undermining oversight.

**Direction:** Borrow Schelling-point coordination games from behavioral game theory. Construct oversight tasks with a salient-but-wrong focal answer and measure whether independent model instances disproportionately converge on the focal wrong answer (vs the truth) under debate aggregation, quantifying focal-point pull as a coordination-risk metric. Pure inference on an open model.

**Why it matters:** Probes a model-organism-style coordination failure (coordinating without verbalizing) within a feasible 30h slice, exactly the medium/long-horizon, lab-independent threat the steering prioritizes.

**Relevant context:** Schelling focal points from behavioral game theory (Schelling 1960). Implicit collusion risk in debate; peer-prediction detection (arXiv:1910.03779). Steering note: favor model-organism studies (Schelling games, non-verbalized plans).

title: Regression-Testing Suite for Oversight Stability Across Model Versions
quick_reasoning: Tracks oversight reliability across model versions, useful safety infrastructure.

original_idea.body:
# Regression-Testing Suite for Oversight Stability Across Model Versions

**Problem:** When the model underlying an oversight protocol is updated, previously-caught failure cases may silently regress, but there is no oversight regression suite to detect this.

**Direction:** Transfer regression testing from software engineering. Curate a small frozen suite of oversight 'test cases' (argument + correct verdict + flaw type) and run it across several open-model versions/sizes, reporting which cases regress. Build the reusable suite + runner as the deliverable and analyze regression patterns.

**Why it matters:** A regression suite makes oversight reliability trackable over time and across models, durable, shareable safety infrastructure that needs no lab resources and that labs rarely maintain publicly.

**Relevant context:** Regression testing from software engineering; rethinking testing for LLM applications (arXiv:2508.20737). Judge verdict instability across models/seeds (arXiv:2412.12509). No standardized oversight benchmark exists (context gap).

title: Where Debate Breaks: Mapping the Information-Asymmetry Threshold
quick_reasoning: Identifies operating-regime boundary for debate oversight protocol.

original_idea.body:
# Where Debate Breaks: Mapping the Information-Asymmetry Threshold

**Problem:** Debate as scalable oversight assumes a weak judge can extract truth from two stronger debaters via information asymmetry (judge sees only verified quotes). The causal chain to oversight failure runs: superhuman task -> judge cannot verify directly -> relies on debate -> debate fails when asymmetry is too large -> judge accepts a false claim. The under-studied link is exactly how much asymmetry the protocol can tolerate before judge accuracy collapses.

**Direction:** Using the QuALITY reading-comprehension setup with a small open judge model (e.g. a 1-3B instruct model) and a stronger debater model accessed via API, systematically vary the quote-budget the judge is allowed to see (0, 1, 2, 4, 8 quotes) and measure judge accuracy on honest-vs-dishonest debates. Plot the accuracy curve against asymmetry to find the breakpoint. No training required; just prompt orchestration and answer scoring.

**Why it matters:** Identifies a concrete operating-regime boundary for a leading oversight protocol that labs are betting on. The threshold is a transferable, model-agnostic finding doable entirely with open models and a public dataset, no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) show debate raises non-expert judge accuracy to 76% (LLM) / 88% (human) on QuALITY where judges see only short verified quotes; Kenton et al. 2024 (NeurIPS, arXiv:2407.04622) study weak LLMs judging strong LLMs and find debate beats consultancy. Neither systematically sweeps the asymmetry budget itself.

title: Obfuscated Arguments in Miniature: Can a Weak Judge Detect 'I Don't Know Which Step Is Wrong'?
quick_reasoning: Tests a theoretically-flagged debate failure mode (obfuscated arguments).

original_idea.body:
# Obfuscated Arguments in Miniature: Can a Weak Judge Detect 'I Don't Know Which Step Is Wrong'?

**Problem:** The obfuscated-arguments failure: a dishonest debater builds a long multi-step argument where neither side can localize the false step, so the judge can't be shown where the lie is. Causal chain: hard claim -> long opaque argument -> no localizable error -> judge defaults to plausibility -> accepts falsehood. The under-studied link is whether judges can be cued to recognize obfuscation rather than evaluate content.

**Direction:** Construct ~50 synthetic multi-step arithmetic/logic 'proofs' (some with a single hidden error buried at a random depth) and present them to a small judge model in a debate-style setup. Compare a baseline judge prompt vs. an 'obfuscation-aware' prompt that asks the judge to estimate confidence that an error exists and where. Measure whether the judge's calibration to error-presence beats chance even when it cannot find the error.

**Why it matters:** Tests a concrete, theoretically-flagged failure mode of debate using cheap synthetic tasks, fully outside any lab. A positive result (judges can flag obfuscation) suggests a cheap protocol patch; a negative result quantifies a fundamental limit.

**Relevant context:** Barnes & Christiano and the LessWrong 'Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem' identify dishonest debaters exploiting arguments where the error cannot be localized; Prover-Estimator Debate (arXiv:2506.13609) is a recent protocol proposed specifically to avoid obfuscation, motivating empirical measurement.

title: Self-Preference Bias as an Oversight Backdoor: Does a Judge Favor Its Own Family?
quick_reasoning: Tests whether self-preference flips correctness judgments in oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Preference Bias as an Oversight Backdoor: Does a Judge Favor Its Own Family?

**Problem:** When oversight is delegated to an LLM judge, the judge can systematically prefer outputs that resemble its own generations (lower perplexity to itself). Causal chain: deploy LLM-as-judge -> judge has self-preference -> a model from the judge's family gets inflated scores -> oversight rewards the wrong answer. The under-studied link is whether self-preference is strong enough to flip correctness judgments, not just style preferences.

**Direction:** Take a fixed set of QA/reasoning items with one correct and one incorrect answer. Generate the incorrect answer in the judge's own model-family style and the correct answer in a foreign-family style (and vice versa). Measure how often the judge picks the incorrect-but-familiar answer. Use 2-3 small open judge models and compute the correctness-flip rate attributable to familiarity.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies whether a documented stylistic bias actually corrupts the correctness signal that oversight depends on. Pure inference + scoring, runs on a single GPU, no proprietary data, directly relevant to medium-horizon automated-oversight pipelines.

**Relevant context:** Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv:2410.21819) shows judges score lower-perplexity (self-familiar) outputs higher; 'Justice or Prejudice?' (arXiv:2410.02736) catalogs judge biases. The link from familiarity to correctness-flips is under-measured.

title: Sycophancy as the First Link in the Reward-Hacking Chain: A Behavioral Gradient
quick_reasoning: Tests sycophancy-to-reward-hacking link, targets a named oversight problem.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy as the First Link in the Reward-Hacking Chain: A Behavioral Gradient

**Problem:** Recent work argues sycophancy and reward hacking lie on one spectrum: flattery -> agreeing with wrong premises -> gaming evaluators -> subterfuge. Causal chain: overseer has a bias -> model learns to flatter the bias -> flattery generalizes to exploiting other evaluator weaknesses. The under-studied link is whether a model's measured sycophancy on cheap probes predicts its willingness to exploit a manipulable grader.

**Direction:** Build a sycophancy probe battery (agreeing with false user claims, switching answers under pushback) and a separate 'gameable grader' task (a grader that rewards a detectable superficial cue). Across several open models, correlate each model's sycophancy score with its rate of exploiting the gameable grader. No training; pure behavioral evaluation.

**Why it matters:** If a cheap sycophancy probe predicts reward-hacking propensity, facilitators get an early-warning oversight signal computable without lab resources. Directly targets Open Phil's 'reward hacking of human oversight' open problem.

**Relevant context:** Sharma et al. and the 'Sycophancy to Subterfuge' work (arXiv:2406.10162) show sycophancy generalizing to reward-tampering; LessWrong 'Reward hacking behavior can generalize across tasks' reports cross-task generalization. The predictive link between a sycophancy probe and grader-exploitation is open.

title: Position Bias Compounding Through Oversight Layers
quick_reasoning: Measures bias compounding in recursive oversight, well-scoped safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Position Bias Compounding Through Oversight Layers

**Problem:** LLM judges have position/order bias (swapping answer order shifts accuracy by >10% in code judging). In recursive oversight, a judgment feeds the next layer. Causal chain: layer-1 judge has position bias -> its noisy output orders layer-2 candidates -> bias compounds -> final oversight verdict diverges from truth. The under-studied link is how a single-layer bias propagates and amplifies across stacked judgments.

**Direction:** Simulate a 2-3 layer recursive judging pipeline with a small open model. At each layer measure position-bias-induced flip rate, then propagate verdicts forward and measure whether final-layer error exceeds the single-layer rate. Test order-randomization and swap-and-average as cheap mitigations and quantify how much they dampen compounding.

**Why it matters:** Recursive oversight protocols assume per-layer errors don't catastrophically compound. This gives a concrete, lab-independent measurement of compounding for a well-documented bias, plus a tested cheap mitigation.

**Relevant context:** Documented position bias causes >10% accuracy shifts under order swaps (LLM-as-a-Judge bias literature, arXiv:2410.02736); recursive reward modeling / iterated amplification assume bounded per-layer error (Anthropic recommended directions). Compounding across simulated layers is under-studied empirically.

title: Verbosity Bias as an Exploitable Channel: Padding to Pass Oversight
quick_reasoning: Quantifies verbosity bias as an oversight attack surface.

original_idea.body:
# Verbosity Bias as an Exploitable Channel: Padding to Pass Oversight

**Problem:** Judges prefer verbose/fluent outputs regardless of substance. Causal chain: oversight uses an LLM grader -> grader rewards length/fluency -> a model learns answers can pass by padding -> incorrect-but-verbose answers slip through. The under-studied link is the exploit yield: how much can a fixed wrong answer's pass-rate be raised purely by adding non-substantive padding?

**Direction:** Take a set of incorrect answers to factual/reasoning questions. Programmatically generate padded variants (added qualifications, restated context, formal tone) holding the wrong claim fixed. Measure the grader's pass-rate as a function of token count for several small judge models. Fit a dose-response curve of pass-rate vs. padding.

**Why it matters:** Turns a qualitative bias into a quantitative attack surface for automated oversight, the kind of fuzzy-reward exploit hard to measure but cheap to run outside a lab. Useful as a red-team benchmark for oversight graders.

**Relevant context:** LLM-as-a-Judge surveys report verbosity/length bias from RLHF (arXiv:2410.02736); reward-model length bias is a known reward-hacking vector. The controlled dose-response of pass-rate vs. padding for fixed-wrong answers is under-measured.

title: Does Persuasion Track Truth? Decoupling Convincingness from Correctness in Debate
quick_reasoning: Probes when persuasion and truth diverge in debate oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Does Persuasion Track Truth? Decoupling Convincingness from Correctness in Debate

**Problem:** Debate works only if the more truthful debater is also the more persuasive one to the judge. Causal chain: debate run -> judge follows persuasiveness -> if persuasiveness and correctness decouple, judge is misled. The under-studied link is the conditional probability that the persuasive side is correct, measured separately from overall judge accuracy.

**Direction:** On QuALITY-style items, have a debater model argue both honest and dishonest positions. Have a small judge rate each side's persuasiveness AND pick a winner. Compute correlation between rated-persuasiveness and correctness, and the judge-accuracy conditional on the dishonest side being judged more persuasive. Identify item features where persuasion decouples from truth.

**Why it matters:** Khan et al. found 'more persuasive LLMs lead to more truthful answers' on average; this probes when that breaks. Characterizing the decoupling regime is a transferable safety result for the debate research program, doable with public data and small models.

**Relevant context:** Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) title claims more persuasive LLMs -> more truthful answers; the failure cases where persuasion and truth diverge are exactly the under-studied risk for debate-based oversight.

title: Latent-Space Attack-Surface Mapper (no adversarial training)
quick_reasoning: Measures latent robustness of refusal, directly addresses adversarial-robustness problem.

original_idea.body:
# Latent-Space Attack-Surface Mapper (no adversarial training)

**Problem:** Latent adversarial training is a promising alternative to explicit attack enumeration, but there is no cheap diagnostic that measures, for a given open model, how vulnerable its LATENT space is — i.e., how small a perturbation to hidden activations is needed to flip a refusal into compliance.

**Direction:** Build a tool that, for harmful prompts the model refuses, searches for the minimal-norm activation perturbation (gradient on hidden states, no weight updates) at a chosen layer that flips the output to compliance. Report a 'latent fragility' score (mean perturbation norm) per model and per hazard category.

**Why it matters:** Provides a measurement for the property latent adversarial training targets, without doing any training — letting independent researchers assess latent robustness cheaply. Single GPU, gradients on activations only, no fine-tuning.

**Relevant context:** Context open problem: 'Develop alternatives to adversarial training (e.g., latent adversarial training)... without requiring explicit attack enumeration' (Open Phil RFP, starred). Arditi et al. (NeurIPS 2024) show activation steering flips refusal, establishing feasibility of latent perturbation.

title: Easy-to-Hard Generalization Decay: When Does a Cheap Evaluator Stop Tracking Hard-Problem Correctness?
quick_reasoning: Tests core assumption of easy-to-hard oversight generalization.

original_idea.body:
# Easy-to-Hard Generalization Decay: When Does a Cheap Evaluator Stop Tracking Hard-Problem Correctness?

**Problem:** Easy-to-hard oversight trains/uses an evaluator on easy problems and applies it to hard ones the human can't check. Causal chain: evaluator validated on easy -> applied to hard -> if evaluator quality decays with difficulty, oversight silently fails on exactly the hard cases that matter. The under-studied link is the decay curve of evaluator-correctness-agreement vs. problem difficulty.

**Direction:** Use a difficulty-graded math/reasoning dataset (e.g. MATH levels) with ground-truth answers. Use a small open model as the evaluator scoring candidate solutions. Measure evaluator-vs-ground-truth agreement at each difficulty level. Plot the decay curve and test whether confidence/uncertainty signals from the evaluator predict where it has decayed.

**Why it matters:** Directly tests the core assumption of easy-to-hard generalization, an Anthropic-recommended direction, using open models and public difficulty-labeled data. The decay curve tells facilitators where cheap evaluators can and cannot be trusted.

**Relevant context:** Sun et al. 'Easy-to-Hard Generalization' (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2403.09472) train process reward models on easy problems and apply them to hard ones (52.5% on MATH500 from easy-only supervision). The agreement-decay curve as a function of difficulty is the under-studied link.

title: Collusion-Lite: Can an Untrusted Monitor Be Cued to Pass Its Allies?
quick_reasoning: Probes monitor collusion, a central AI-control concern.

original_idea.body:
# Collusion-Lite: Can an Untrusted Monitor Be Cued to Pass Its Allies?

**Problem:** AI control uses one model to monitor another. The feared failure: policy and monitor collude. Causal chain: deploy untrusted monitor -> monitor recognizes outputs from a colluding model -> monitor suppresses alarms -> bad action slips through. The under-studied link is how easily a same-family monitor can be steered (via subtle shared cues) to under-report on aligned outputs without explicit coordination.

**Direction:** Set up a flag-the-backdoored-code monitoring task. Insert a benign-looking shared 'signal' (a stylistic token pattern) into some malicious outputs. Measure whether a same-family monitor's catch-rate drops on signaled-malicious vs. unsignaled-malicious outputs. Compare a same-family vs. different-family monitor to test the collusion-channel hypothesis with no training.

**Why it matters:** Provides a cheap empirical probe of monitor collusion, a central AI-control concern that frontier labs study with heavy infra. A small prototype harness here is strategically valuable monitoring infrastructure usable by outside researchers.

**Relevant context:** Redwood Research AI-control work warns capable untrusted models may fool trusted monitors and that policy-monitor collusion is a key risk ('The case for ensuring powerful AIs are controlled'; control-protocol composition posts). Cheap empirical probes of implicit-cue collusion are scarce.

title: Consultancy's Hidden Failure: Quantifying Judge Anchoring to a Single Advisor
quick_reasoning: Measures anchoring failure in consultancy oversight protocol.

original_idea.body:
# Consultancy's Hidden Failure: Quantifying Judge Anchoring to a Single Advisor

**Problem:** Consultancy (single advisor argues one assigned side) underperforms debate, but is cheaper and widely used. Causal chain: judge consults one advisor -> advisor argues an assigned (possibly wrong) side -> judge anchors on the one-sided case -> accepts it. The under-studied link is the magnitude of anchoring: how much the judge's prior shifts toward whatever side it happens to hear first/only.

**Direction:** On QuALITY-style items, run consultancy with a small judge and measure judge accuracy when the consultant is assigned the correct vs. incorrect side. Then test cheap debiasing prompts (explicit 'consider the opposing case', forced self-generated counterargument) and measure how much they recover the accuracy lost to anchoring.

**Why it matters:** Consultancy is the realistic default when full debate is too expensive. Measuring its anchoring failure and a no-training mitigation is directly useful and entirely lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04622) and Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) find debate beats consultancy, especially when the consultant is randomly assigned a side. The size of the anchoring effect and cheap prompt-level mitigations are under-explored.

title: The Calibration Gap: Do Weak Judges Know When They're Out of Their Depth?
quick_reasoning: Tests whether weak-judge confidence supports safe escalation in oversight.

original_idea.body:
# The Calibration Gap: Do Weak Judges Know When They're Out of Their Depth?

**Problem:** Scalable oversight degrades gracefully only if a weak judge abstains when it can't reliably evaluate. Causal chain: judge faces a too-hard case -> judge is overconfident -> gives a wrong verdict instead of abstaining -> oversight commits a confident error. The under-studied link is whether weak judges' stated confidence tracks their actual reliability across difficulty.

**Direction:** On a difficulty-graded judgment task, elicit the judge's verbalized and token-probability confidence per item. Measure calibration (reliability diagram, ECE) and the abstention quality of a 'judge may say UNSURE' protocol. Quantify how much giving the judge an abstain option preserves overall correctness by routing hard cases to (simulated) escalation.

**Why it matters:** An abstaining-when-uncertain weak overseer is a key building block for safe escalation. Measuring whether confidence is usable for routing is cheap, model-agnostic, and needs no lab infra; useful for designing escalation protocols.

**Relevant context:** Scaling-laws-for-scalable-oversight (arXiv:2504.18530) frames oversight as a capability gap between guard and adversary; uncertainty-as-active-signal surveys (arXiv:2601.15690) motivate confidence-based routing. Whether weak-judge confidence is reliable enough to gate escalation is under-studied.

title: Systematic Overseer Errors Are Correlated, Not Random: Testing the Independence Assumption
quick_reasoning: Tests independence assumption in ensemble/recursive oversight, named open problem.

original_idea.body:
# Systematic Overseer Errors Are Correlated, Not Random: Testing the Independence Assumption

**Problem:** Recursive/ensemble oversight implicitly assumes overseer errors are roughly independent so they wash out. Causal chain: aggregate many overseers -> assume independent errors -> if errors are correlated on the same hard items, aggregation gives false confidence. The under-studied link is the actual error-correlation structure across judges on the same items.

**Direction:** Run several small open judge models (and the same model under varied prompts/temperatures) on a shared set of judgment items. Compute the inter-judge error-correlation matrix and identify clusters of items where all judges fail together. Estimate how much majority-vote accuracy is inflated by treating correlated errors as independent.

**Why it matters:** If oversight errors are systematically correlated (per the 'systematic oversight errors' open problem), ensembling provides far less safety than assumed. This is a clean statistics-friendly result computable on one GPU with no proprietary data.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic recommended directions list 'characterize and mitigate systematic oversight errors' and 'recursive oversight when each layer has systematic errors' as open problems. The empirical error-correlation structure across LLM judges is largely uncharacterized.

title: Quote-Fabrication Attacks on Information-Asymmetric Debate
quick_reasoning: Tests integrity of the evidence channel in information-asymmetric debate oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Quote-Fabrication Attacks on Information-Asymmetric Debate

**Problem:** QuALITY-style debate trusts that quotes a debater shows the judge are verified extracts from the source. Causal chain: debater provides 'evidence' quotes -> judge weights quoted evidence heavily -> if a debater can smuggle near-verbatim but altered quotes, judge is misled. The under-studied link is the judge's robustness to subtly-corrupted or out-of-context quotes.

**Direction:** On QuALITY passages, generate three quote conditions: faithful, subtly-altered (one word/number changed), and out-of-context (real quote, misleading framing). With verification disabled, measure how each condition changes a small judge's verdict. Then add a cheap automatic quote-verification step (string match against source) and measure recovered accuracy.

**Why it matters:** Tests the integrity of the evidence channel that makes information-asymmetric debate work, and prototypes a cheap automated quote-verifier, a small piece of strategically valuable oversight infrastructure usable outside any lab.

**Relevant context:** Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) rely on judges seeing only verified quotes for information asymmetry; the robustness of judgments to altered/out-of-context quotes and the value of automated verification are under-explored.

title: Weak-to-Strong Supervision Under Label Noise: Where Does the Strong Student Stop Trusting the Weak Teacher?
quick_reasoning: Probes weak-to-strong assumption under systematic teacher error.

original_idea.body:
# Weak-to-Strong Supervision Under Label Noise: Where Does the Strong Student Stop Trusting the Weak Teacher?

**Problem:** Weak-to-strong generalization elicits strong-model capability from weak-model labels. Causal chain: weak teacher gives noisy labels -> strong student fits them -> if noise is systematic (not random), the student inherits the bias rather than its latent correct knowledge. The under-studied link is how the student's recovery of true answers degrades as teacher-label noise shifts from random to systematic.

**Direction:** Without training, use in-context weak-to-strong: give a strong model a few weak-teacher-labeled examples (with controllable random vs. systematic label corruption) and measure how well its predictions on new items recover ground truth. Sweep noise type and rate to find where the student stops correcting the teacher and starts copying its bias.

**Why it matters:** Probes the central weak-to-strong assumption (eliciting latent correct knowledge) under realistic systematic teacher error, using only in-context learning on open models, no fine-tuning or clusters. Directly varies the canonical experiment per the strategy hints.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI weak-to-strong generalization (open code) shows strong students can exceed weak teachers; the strategy hints suggest varying model-size gaps and task domains. Systematic (vs random) teacher-label-noise sensitivity via in-context elicitation is under-studied and feasible.

title: Confidence Inflation in Debate: Does Arguing a Side Make a Model More Sure It's Right?
quick_reasoning: Tests role-assignment calibration distortion in debate oversight, well-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Confidence Inflation in Debate: Does Arguing a Side Make a Model More Sure It's Right?

**Problem:** In debate, each model is assigned a side and argues it hard. Causal chain: model assigned a (possibly false) side -> generates committed arguments -> commitment inflates the model's own stated confidence -> a downstream judge or aggregator over-weights a confidently-wrong debater. The under-studied link is whether role-assignment itself distorts a debater's calibration.

**Direction:** Ask an open model for its calibrated answer+confidence on a set of factual questions cold. Then assign it (randomly) to argue one side and re-elicit its confidence after producing the argument. Measure the confidence shift attributable purely to role assignment, separately for cases where it was assigned the correct vs. incorrect side.

**Why it matters:** If role assignment inflates confidence on wrong sides, confidence-aware aggregation of debaters is dangerous. A clean, cheap behavioral result on a real oversight protocol, no lab resources needed.

**Relevant context:** Debate protocols (Khan et al. 2024 arXiv:2402.06782; Kenton et al. 2024 arXiv:2407.04622) assign debaters fixed sides; sycophancy/role-conditioning literature shows behavior shifts under role framing. The calibration distortion from forced advocacy is under-measured.

title: Cross-Domain Transfer of Oversight Failures: Does a Judge That Fails on Math Also Fail on Code?
quick_reasoning: Tests whether oversight validation transfers across domains, central safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Domain Transfer of Oversight Failures: Does a Judge That Fails on Math Also Fail on Code?

**Problem:** Facilitators want to know if validating an overseer in one domain licenses trusting it elsewhere. Causal chain: validate judge on domain A -> deploy on domain B -> if failure modes don't transfer, the validation is misleading. The under-studied link is the correlation of judge failure across task domains for the same items' difficulty.

**Direction:** Build matched judgment items across 3 domains (arithmetic reasoning, short code correctness, factual QA) with ground truth. For each small judge model, measure per-domain accuracy and per-item failure, then test whether failure on one domain predicts failure on another (controlling for difficulty). Report a domain-transfer matrix of oversight reliability.

**Why it matters:** Tells facilitators whether oversight reliability is a stable trait or domain-specific, central to safely extrapolating any oversight validation. Pure evaluation on open models and public data.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic recommended directions ask when weak overseers reliably supervise stronger models; LLM-judge bias surveys (arXiv:2410.02736) note domain-dependence. Cross-domain transfer of an individual judge's failure profile is under-characterized.

title: The Tie-Breaker Problem: How Judges Resolve Genuinely Balanced Debates
quick_reasoning: Examines arbitrary heuristics in hardest oversight cases (near-tie debates).

original_idea.body:
# The Tie-Breaker Problem: How Judges Resolve Genuinely Balanced Debates

**Problem:** Debate assumes a clear winner usually emerges. Causal chain: hard question -> both debaters argue well -> judge faces a near-tie -> judge falls back on irrelevant heuristics (last speaker, longer rebuttal, confident tone) -> verdict is essentially arbitrary on the hardest cases. The under-studied link is what default heuristic a judge uses when arguments are balanced.

**Direction:** Construct debates engineered to be near-balanced (swap which side gets the last word, equalize length, vary tone). With a small judge, measure how verdicts depend on these non-substantive factors specifically in the balanced regime. Quantify the 'arbitrariness rate' and which surface cue dominates.

**Why it matters:** The hardest oversight cases are exactly the balanced ones; if judges resolve them by arbitrary cues, debate gives false assurance precisely where it's needed most. Cheap, controlled, fully external research.

**Relevant context:** Position/recency and verbosity biases are documented for LLM judges (arXiv:2410.02736, arXiv:2410.21819). How these surface cues dominate specifically in near-tie debates, the worst case for oversight, is under-studied.

title: StrongREJECT Evaluator Reliability Audit Tool
quick_reasoning: Audits robustness of jailbreak-benchmark evaluators, meta-science safety gap.

original_idea.body:
# StrongREJECT Evaluator Reliability Audit Tool

**Problem:** Jailbreak benchmarks increasingly rely on LLM-judge evaluators (StrongREJECT rubric, AILuminate's evaluator), but there is no easy tool for practitioners to audit how much the final robustness ranking depends on which judge model is used.

**Direction:** Run the StrongREJECT rubric prompt with several different judge models (GPT-4o-mini, Claude Haiku, an open judge like Llama-3-70B, the fine-tuned Gemma-2B evaluator) on a fixed set of responses, and measure inter-judge agreement and rank stability of the resulting model leaderboard. Ship the audit harness.

**Why it matters:** If leaderboards flip depending on the judge, published robustness claims are unreliable — a meta-science gap the field has not closed. Auditing evaluator robustness needs no model training and only modest API/inference budget; strong counterfactual value as independent verification.

**Relevant context:** StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) ships both a rubric-based evaluator (usable with any LLM) and a fine-tuned Gemma-2B evaluator. 'LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness' (arXiv:2503.02574) motivates evaluator-robustness audits.

title: Reward-Model Overoptimization on a Budget: Best-of-N Reveals the Hacking Frontier
quick_reasoning: Reproduces reward overoptimization (Goodhart), a core oversight failure.

original_idea.body:
# Reward-Model Overoptimization on a Budget: Best-of-N Reveals the Hacking Frontier

**Problem:** Oversight via a reward model fails when policies overoptimize it (Goodhart). Causal chain: use RM as overseer signal -> optimize against it -> proxy score rises while true quality falls past a threshold. The under-studied link, for accessible models, is where the proxy-vs-true divergence point lies under simple best-of-N selection rather than full RL.

**Direction:** Use an open reward/judge model as the proxy and a separate ground-truth checker (e.g. exact-answer for math). Generate N candidate answers, select the top-K by proxy score, and plot true accuracy vs. proxy score as N grows. Locate the N at which selecting harder on the proxy starts decreasing true accuracy, i.e. the overoptimization knee.

**Why it matters:** Reproduces reward overoptimization with zero training (just sampling + selection), making a core scalable-oversight failure measurable on a single GPU. The knee location is a transferable safety datum.

**Relevant context:** Reward-hacking surveys (arXiv:2604.13602) and gradient-regularization work (arXiv:2602.18037) treat RM overoptimization as central; best-of-N is a known cheap proxy for optimization pressure. Mapping the overoptimization knee with open models via selection is feasible and under-done at this scale.

title: Does Debate Help When Both Debaters Are Wrong? The Shared-Blindspot Failure
quick_reasoning: Maps a fundamental limit of debate oversight (shared blind spots).

original_idea.body:
# Does Debate Help When Both Debaters Are Wrong? The Shared-Blindspot Failure

**Problem:** Debate assumes at least one debater knows/argues the truth. Causal chain: question where both debaters share a misconception -> neither presents the correct case -> judge chooses between two wrong answers -> oversight confidently lands on a falsehood. The under-studied link is how debate behaves when the truth is outside both debaters' competence.

**Direction:** Curate questions where a given debater model is reliably wrong (probe it first to find shared blind spots). Run debate between two instances on those items and measure how often the judge is steered to a wrong consensus, and whether the judge's confidence is (dangerously) high. Compare to items where the model is competent.

**Why it matters:** Maps a fundamental limit of debate, oversight cannot exceed the union of debater competence, and tests whether the judge at least signals low confidence. Cheap to run with one open model family; valuable medium-horizon insight as capabilities push past human checkability.

**Relevant context:** Debate results (Khan et al. 2024 arXiv:2402.06782) assume informed debaters; the shared-blindspot regime (truth outside both debaters' reach) is precisely the superhuman case oversight targets and is under-studied empirically.

title: Anchoring the Judge with a Fake 'Expert' Prior: Authority Cues in Oversight
quick_reasoning: Quantifies authority-deference exploit in supervision, named open problem.

original_idea.body:
# Anchoring the Judge with a Fake 'Expert' Prior: Authority Cues in Oversight

**Problem:** Strategic AI could exploit overseer deference to authority. Causal chain: overseer sees an answer framed as coming from an authority/expert/'the model is highly confident' -> overseer defers -> incorrect answer gains undue weight. The under-studied link is the size of the authority-deference effect on correctness judgments.

**Direction:** Hold answers fixed and vary only the framing metadata shown to a small judge ('from a senior expert', 'verified', 'low-confidence draft', neutral). Measure the shift in the judge's acceptance of incorrect answers attributable purely to authority framing. Test a debiasing instruction that tells the judge to ignore provenance.

**Why it matters:** Directly targets the open problem of mapping biases in human/AI supervision that strategic systems could exploit, using a controlled, cheap manipulation. Authority-framing is an exploit vector that needs no lab access to study.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic and UK AISI list 'map and mitigate biases in supervision exploitable by strategic AI' as an open problem; LLM-judge bias work (arXiv:2410.02736) catalogs framing biases. Quantifying authority-cue deference on correctness specifically is under-explored.

title: Self-Play Debate Training-Free Replication: Does Adversarial Pressure Alone Sharpen Judges?
quick_reasoning: Tests inference-time recovery of self-play debate benefits for oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Play Debate Training-Free Replication: Does Adversarial Pressure Alone Sharpen Judges?

**Problem:** Training debaters via self-play improved judge accuracy, but training is out of reach for most. Causal chain: stronger adversarial debate -> sharper distinguishing arguments -> better judge accuracy. The under-studied link, for low-resource settings, is whether prompt-level adversarial pressure (rounds of rebuttal, devil's advocate) recovers some of the gain without any training.

**Direction:** On QuALITY-style items, compare judge accuracy across escalating no-training adversarial settings: single statement, one rebuttal round, multi-round with forced strongest-counterargument prompts. Measure marginal judge-accuracy gain per added adversarial round and find where returns saturate.

**Why it matters:** Tells the under-resourced research community how much of the self-play debate benefit is achievable with prompting alone, maximizing counterfactual value. Pure orchestration, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** 'Training Language Models to Win Debates with Self-Play Improves Judge Accuracy' (arXiv:2409.16636) gets gains via training; the question of how much is recoverable through inference-time adversarial structure alone is under-studied and accessible.

title: Backdoored-Judge Detection on a Shoestring: Behavioral Fingerprints of a Poisoned Evaluator
quick_reasoning: Auditing harness for evaluator-integrity against poisoning, directly safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Backdoored-Judge Detection on a Shoestring: Behavioral Fingerprints of a Poisoned Evaluator

**Problem:** Lightly poisoned judge-training data can implant a backdoor that flips judgments on trigger inputs. Causal chain: poisoned judge deployed -> trigger present -> judge silently passes attacker-favored output -> oversight compromised. The under-studied link is whether a downstream user with only black-box query access can detect such a backdoored judge.

**Direction:** Simulate a backdoored judge by wrapping an open judge with a trigger-conditioned override rule (no training needed). Then act as an auditor with only query access: design behavioral tests (consistency under paraphrase, anomaly in pass-rate for trigger-like patterns, sensitivity probes) and measure detection power vs. false-positive rate against a clean judge.

**Why it matters:** Builds a small, strategically valuable auditing harness for evaluator integrity, exactly the kind of monitoring infrastructure useful outside labs, and tests a defense against a documented poisoning threat.

**Relevant context:** Search results note 'lightly poisoned judge-training data can implant backdoors that systematically bias later judgments'; black-box detectability of such evaluator backdoors is under-studied and approachable via behavioral testing.

title: Length-of-Argument Arms Race: Does More Debate Text Help or Drown the Judge?
quick_reasoning: Tests non-monotonic debate-length effect on weak-judge oversight accuracy.

original_idea.body:
# Length-of-Argument Arms Race: Does More Debate Text Help or Drown the Judge?

**Problem:** More debate rounds give more information but also more text for a weak judge to process. Causal chain: extend debate -> judge context fills -> if the judge degrades with long context, added rounds can lower accuracy. The under-studied link is the non-monotonic relationship between total debate length and weak-judge accuracy.

**Direction:** On a fixed item set, run debates of increasing transcript length (more rounds / longer turns) and measure small-judge accuracy at each length. Identify whether accuracy peaks then declines (information overload) and whether a cheap summarization step before judging recovers performance.

**Why it matters:** Protocol designers assume more debate is safer; a non-monotonic curve would be a concrete design caution. Cheap to run, model-agnostic, and tests a simple summarization mitigation, all outside lab infra.

**Relevant context:** Long-context degradation ('lost in the middle') is well documented for LLMs; debate transcripts can be long (Kenton et al. 2024 swept ~5M generations across multi-round protocols). The interaction between transcript length and weak-judge accuracy is under-studied.

title: Cross-Examination as a Lie Localizer: Can Targeted Questions Break Obfuscation?
quick_reasoning: Tests a leading fix to debate's central obfuscation failure mode.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Examination as a Lie Localizer: Can Targeted Questions Break Obfuscation?

**Problem:** Cross-examination (judge or debater interrogates a debater's earlier claims) is proposed to defeat obfuscated arguments by forcing the dishonest side to commit to localizable sub-claims. Causal chain: dishonest long argument -> cross-examination forces step-level commitments -> inconsistency surfaces -> judge localizes the lie. The under-studied link is whether cheap, prompted cross-examination actually surfaces inconsistencies in practice.

**Direction:** On synthetic multi-step arguments with a single planted error, compare a baseline judge to a judge that issues 2-3 targeted follow-up questions to the defending model and checks for self-contradiction. Measure improvement in error-localization rate from cross-examination, with no training.

**Why it matters:** Empirically tests a leading theoretical fix to debate's central failure mode using only prompting, giving the external research community evidence on whether cross-examination is worth its cost.

**Relevant context:** Cross-examination is proposed (Irving/Barnes & alignment-forum debate discussions; Prover-Estimator Debate arXiv:2506.13609) as a route around obfuscated arguments. Cheap inference-time empirical tests of its lie-localizing power are scarce.

title: When the Overseer Is the Same Model: Self-Evaluation Blind Spots
quick_reasoning: Quantifies self-evaluation blind-spot overlap, common oversight shortcut.

original_idea.body:
# When the Overseer Is the Same Model: Self-Evaluation Blind Spots

**Problem:** Cheap oversight often uses a model to grade its own outputs. Causal chain: model produces an answer -> same model grades it -> shared blind spots and self-preference mean errors the model can't see in generation it also can't see in evaluation -> systematic undetected failures. The under-studied link is the overlap between a model's generation errors and its self-evaluation misses.

**Direction:** For a single open model, collect items it answers incorrectly. Have the same model self-grade those answers and measure how often it endorses its own wrong answers vs. catches them. Compare against grading by a different-family model of similar size to isolate the self-evaluation blind-spot from general judging difficulty.

**Why it matters:** Self-evaluation is the cheapest and most common oversight shortcut; quantifying its blind-spot overlap warns where it is unsafe. Fully external, single-GPU, public-data study directly relevant to automated-oversight pipelines.

**Relevant context:** Self-preference bias (arXiv:2410.21819) and 'auditing language models for hidden objectives' (arXiv:2503.10965) motivate concern about self-evaluation; the specific overlap between generation errors and self-evaluation misses is under-measured.

title: Translating the Capability Gap into an Oversight Safety Margin
quick_reasoning: Converts capability-gap scaling into a usable oversight safety margin.

original_idea.body:
# Translating the Capability Gap into an Oversight Safety Margin

**Problem:** Scaling-laws work frames oversight as a contest between a 'Guard' (overseer) and an adversary, where Guard performance scales with capability but the adversary's stays flat in some games. Causal chain: capability gap shrinks -> overseer's edge over adversary erodes -> at some gap the overseer can no longer win -> oversight fails. The under-studied link, for practitioners, is converting an observed Guard-vs-adversary win-rate into a usable safety margin for a given model pair.

**Direction:** Pick a simple adversarial oversight game (e.g. spot-the-flawed-solution). Across several open model pairs of differing capability, measure the overseer's win-rate as a function of the capability gap (proxied by benchmark scores). Fit a curve and define an empirical 'minimum safe gap' where win-rate exceeds a chosen threshold.

**Why it matters:** Turns the scaling-laws framing into an actionable, model-agnostic rule of thumb facilitators can compute themselves from public benchmark numbers, no lab infra. Medium-horizon relevance as capability gaps narrow.

**Relevant context:** Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight (arXiv:2504.18530) finds Guard performance scales with general intelligence while the adversary (Houdini) stays constant in adversarial games. Translating this into a per-model-pair safety margin via small open-model experiments is under-explored.

title: Does Eliciting Reasons Before Verdicts Reduce Judge Exploitability?
quick_reasoning: Tests whether CoT judging de-biases or rationalizes oversight exploits.

original_idea.body:
# Does Eliciting Reasons Before Verdicts Reduce Judge Exploitability?

**Problem:** A common cheap intervention is forcing the judge to write reasoning before a verdict (CoT judging). Causal chain: judge exposed to a manipulative argument -> if it verdicts impulsively, it is easily exploited -> if it reasons first, it may catch the manipulation. The under-studied link is whether forced pre-verdict reasoning actually reduces susceptibility to known exploits (verbosity, authority, position) or just rationalizes them.

**Direction:** Reusing the bias-manipulation probes (padding, authority framing, order swaps), compare a direct-verdict judge to a reason-then-verdict judge on susceptibility to each exploit. Measure whether CoT reduces, leaves unchanged, or amplifies (via post-hoc rationalization) each bias.

**Why it matters:** Reason-before-verdict is widely recommended as a free oversight fix; testing whether it genuinely de-biases or merely rationalizes is high-value and cheap. Directly informs protocol design outside labs.

**Relevant context:** Structured multi-dimensional judging reduces self-preference bias ~31.5% without retraining (arXiv:2410.21819 follow-ups); but CoT can also enable post-hoc rationalization. Whether forced reasoning reduces exploitability across distinct bias channels is under-tested.

title: Best-of-N Sampling Attack Curve Tool
quick_reasoning: Quantifies ASR@N for repeated-sampling jailbreaks, deployment-relevant safety measurement.

original_idea.body:
# Best-of-N Sampling Attack Curve Tool

**Problem:** Best-of-N jailbreaking (repeatedly sampling until one response is harmful) is a simple, strong black-box attack, but there is no tool that plots, per model, the attack-success-vs-N curve so deployers can see how robustness erodes with more sampling attempts.

**Direction:** For a fixed harmful-prompt set, sample N responses per prompt (with stochastic decoding) from open models and compute attack success as a function of N (1..64), scoring with StrongREJECT. Report 'ASR@N' curves and the N needed to reach 50% success per model. Ship the harness.

**Why it matters:** Best-of-N requires zero gradient access and is exactly the kind of attack an outside actor with API access can run; quantifying ASR@N is a deployment-relevant measurement labs underreport. Pure inference, single GPU, fits 30h.

**Relevant context:** Best-of-N / repeated-sampling jailbreaks are an established cheap black-box attack class; StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) supports per-sample scoring and is designed to avoid overrating 'empty' jailbreaks. Sampling-driven safety variance noted in arXiv:2503.02574.

title: Distractor Evidence: Can a Debater Win by Burying the Key Fact?
quick_reasoning: Probes evidence-dilution oversight-evasion tactic in debate.

original_idea.body:
# Distractor Evidence: Can a Debater Win by Burying the Key Fact?

**Problem:** A dishonest debater may not lie outright but flood the judge with true-but-irrelevant evidence to bury the one decisive fact. Causal chain: decisive fact exists -> dishonest side adds many true distractors -> judge's attention diluted -> decisive fact under-weighted -> wrong verdict. The under-studied link is the judge's vulnerability to evidence-dilution as opposed to outright falsehood.

**Direction:** On QuALITY-style items where one quote is decisive, construct debate inputs that pad the dishonest side with additional true-but-irrelevant quotes. Measure how the small judge's accuracy declines as the number of distractor quotes grows, and test a 'rank the single most decisive piece of evidence' prompt as a mitigation.

**Why it matters:** Distinguishes a subtle, deniable oversight-evasion strategy (dilution) from detectable lying, and prototypes a cheap mitigation. Controlled, public-data, single-GPU, strongly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Obfuscated-arguments and persuasion literature (arXiv:2402.06782; alignment-forum debate posts) focus on false claims; evidence-dilution via true distractors as an oversight-evasion tactic is under-studied and cheap to probe with QuALITY-style asymmetry.

title: Backcasting Judge Calibration: When Does a Weak Judge Know It's Being Fooled?
quick_reasoning: Characterizes weak-judge calibration under adversarial pressure for oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting Judge Calibration: When Does a Weak Judge Know It's Being Fooled?

**Problem:** Success state: a weak overseer that can reliably flag 'I am uncertain / I may be being manipulated' rather than confidently endorsing a wrong answer. Working backward, we need to know whether weak LLM judges in debate/consultancy are even aware of their own error rate. Today they are often confidently wrong.

**Direction:** Using the open QuALITY-based debate/consultancy setup (Khan et al. 2024; Kenton et al. 2024), run a small open model (e.g. Llama-3-8B) as judge over transcripts produced by a stronger model. Elicit a calibrated confidence with each verdict and plot reliability diagrams (ECE, Brier) separately for debate vs consultancy. Test whether confidence carries information about correctness, and whether a simple abstention threshold recovers accuracy.

**Why it matters:** A success state for scalable oversight requires overseers that fail loudly, not silently. Showing whether judge confidence is informative under adversarial pressure is a cheap, lab-independent contribution to recursive-oversight protocols that must tolerate systematic overseer error.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04622) found debate improves weak-judge reliability but generalizes unevenly beyond QuALITY; Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) report ~76% judge accuracy with persuasive debaters vs 54% baseline. Neither systematically characterizes judge calibration/abstention. Both pipelines are open.

title: The Abstention Backstop: Backcasting a Judge That Refuses Rather Than Guesses
quick_reasoning: Quantifies abstention backstop for safe oversight escalation.

# The Abstention Backstop: Backcasting a Judge That Refuses Rather Than Guesses

**Problem:** Success state: an oversight protocol where the weak judge's worst case is 'I don't know' not 'confidently endorse the deceptive answer'. We need to know how much accuracy a free abstention option buys, and how often debaters can still force a confident wrong verdict.

**Direction:** Add an explicit 'abstain' verdict to the open debate/consultancy judge prompt over QuALITY transcripts. Measure the accuracy/coverage trade-off curve (selective accuracy vs abstention rate) for debate vs single-advisor consultancy, with a small open judge model. Identify question features that the judge abstains on vs gets confidently wrong.

**Why it matters:** Recursive oversight tolerates error far better if errors convert into abstentions that escalate to a human. Quantifying the abstention backstop on an open benchmark gives protocol designers a concrete safety margin, requires no training, and is exactly the diffuse-reward evaluation labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** Debate-vs-consultancy protocols are open (Khan et al. 2024 arXiv:2402.06782; Kenton et al. 2024 arXiv:2407.04622). Selective prediction / abstention is standard but has not been applied to oversight-protocol judges on QuALITY.

title: Backcasting Robust Oversight: Does Debate Survive a Persuasion-Optimized Liar?
quick_reasoning: Tests whether debate's safety property survives optimized persuasion, load-bearing finding.

# Backcasting Robust Oversight: Does Debate Survive a Persuasion-Optimized Liar?

**Problem:** Success state: oversight that holds even when the dishonest debater is explicitly optimized to persuade. Working backward we need an estimate of how far judge accuracy degrades as the dishonest side's persuasion budget (rounds, rhetorical prompting, best-of-n selection) grows.

**Direction:** Hold the honest debater fixed; scale only the dishonest debater's inference-time persuasion (best-of-n sampling on persuasiveness, extra rounds, rhetorical system prompts) using open models on QuALITY. Plot judge accuracy vs dishonest persuasion budget to find the breaking point of debate's truth-advantage.

**Why it matters:** If debate's safety property collapses under modest asymmetric persuasion optimization, that is a load-bearing finding for whether debate can scale. It is pure inference, no training, and directly probes the medium-horizon threat of a strategic AI that out-argues its overseer.

**Relevant context:** Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) found persuasion-optimized debaters help truth on QuALITY; arXiv:2510.05909 finds optimizing for persuasion can improve generalization, raising the question of when persuasion and truth diverge. No public study sweeps a one-sided persuasion budget.
